obligations.instrument: Corporations Act 2001 (Cth)
obligations.citation: s 180(1) (care and diligence); s 180(2) (business judgment rule)
obligations.title: Directors' and officers' care and diligence, including over AI
obligations.statement: Section 180(1) provides that 'A director or other officer of a corporation must exercise their powers and discharge their duties with the degree of care and diligence that a reasonable person would exercise' in the corporation's circumstances and office. Section 180(2) treats a business judgment as meeting that standard where the director or officer makes it in good faith for a proper purpose, has no material personal interest, informs themselves to the extent they reasonably believe appropriate, and rationally believes it is in the corporation's best interests. The provision does not mention AI; it addresses how directors and officers oversee and decide, including on the adoption and control of AI.
obligations.confidenceNote: Text quoted from the 17 March 2025 compilation on the Federal Register of Legislation; a later compilation may exist but s 180 has not been amended in substance. Applies to corporations under the Act; not-for-profits that are companies limited by guarantee are corporations, other not-for-profits are not, so counsel decides reach. Whether a particular AI decision meets s 180 is for counsel.

obligations.instrument: Competition and Consumer Act 2010 (Cth), Schedule 2 (Australian Consumer Law)
obligations.citation: ACL s 18(1) (misleading or deceptive conduct); s 29(1)(a), (g) (false or misleading representations)
obligations.title: Misleading conduct and false representations, including by or about AI
obligations.statement: ACL s 18(1) provides that 'A person must not, in trade or commerce, engage in conduct that is misleading or deceptive or is likely to mislead or deceive.' Section 29(1) addresses false or misleading representations in connection with the supply of goods or services, including that goods are of 'a particular standard, quality, value, grade' (para (a)) and that goods or services have 'sponsorship, approval, performance characteristics' they do not have (para (g)); a pecuniary penalty may be imposed for a contravention of s 29(1). These provisions reach statements a business makes about its AI, and statements an AI system makes to consumers on the business's behalf.
obligations.confidenceNote: Operative words quoted from the 27 August 2026 compilation. The link to AI-generated statements and AI claims is an analytical mapping, not words in the Act. Financial services are covered by the parallel ASIC Act provisions (ss 12DA, 12DB), not researched here.

obligations.instrument: Cyber Security Act 2024 (Cth)
obligations.citation: s 26 (application: reporting business entities); s 27 (ransomware payment report within 72 hours)
obligations.title: Ransomware payment reporting within 72 hours
obligations.statement: Section 27(1) provides that a reporting business entity 'must give the designated Commonwealth body a report' within '72 hours of making the ransomware payment or becoming aware that the ransomware payment has been made'; a contravention attracts a civil penalty of 60 penalty units (s 27(5)). Under s 26 a reporting business entity is one carrying on business in Australia with an annual turnover above the threshold set by the rules, or a responsible entity for a critical infrastructure asset to which Part 2B of the SOCI Act applies. The provision reaches incidents affecting AI systems as it does any other system.
obligations.confidenceNote: Quoted from the Act as made. The turnover threshold is in the Cyber Security (Ransomware Payment Reporting) Rules 2025 (F2025L00278), not fetched. Part 3 commencement date not recorded: the Proclamation was not fetched (open question). Mapping to AI use cases is analytical.

obligations.instrument: Security of Critical Infrastructure Act 2018 (Cth)
obligations.citation: Part 2A: s 30AC (adopt and maintain a CIRMP); s 30AH(1) (purpose of the program); s 30AG(2)(f) (annual report approved by the board)
obligations.title: Critical infrastructure risk management program covering hazards, including from AI
obligations.statement: Section 30AC provides that the responsible entity for one or more critical infrastructure assets 'must: (a) adopt; and (b) maintain; a critical infrastructure risk management program'. Under s 30AH(1) the program's purpose is, for each asset, to 'identify each hazard where there is a material risk that the occurrence of the hazard could have a relevant impact on the asset', and so far as reasonably practicable to minimise or eliminate that risk and mitigate the impact. The annual report on the program is to be approved by the board, council or other governing body where there is one (s 30AG(2)(f)). Hazards from AI systems used in operating an asset fall within this hazard-based approach.
obligations.confidenceNote: Part 2A applies only to assets specified under s 30AB and the rules (Security of Critical Infrastructure (Critical infrastructure risk management program) Rules (LIN 23/006) 2023, not fetched). The AI mapping is analytical; the Act is hazard-based and does not mention AI.

obligations.instrument: Security of Critical Infrastructure Act 2018 (Cth)
obligations.citation: Part 2B: s 30BC (critical cyber security incidents, 12 hours); s 30BD (other cyber security incidents, 72 hours)
obligations.title: Mandatory cyber security incident reporting for critical infrastructure
obligations.statement: Under s 30BC the responsible entity for a critical infrastructure asset notifies a critical cyber security incident 'as soon as practicable, and in any event within 12 hours, after the entity becomes so aware' (s 30BC(1)(d)); under s 30BD other cyber security incidents with a relevant impact are notified 'as soon as practicable, and in any event within 72 hours' (s 30BD(1)(d)). Incidents affecting AI systems that support the asset are reported on the same terms.
obligations.confidenceNote: Timeframes quoted from s 30BC(1)(d) and s 30BD(1)(d). Part 2B applies to assets specified under the Act and rules. AI mapping is analytical.

obligations.instrument: Privacy Act 1988 (Cth), Schedule 2 (statutory tort for serious invasions of privacy), inserted by the Privacy and Other Legislation Amendment Act 2024
obligations.citation: Schedule 2 (cause of action for serious invasions of privacy)
obligations.title: Statutory tort for serious invasions of privacy
obligations.statement: The OAIC states that a statutory tort for serious invasions of privacy, 'contained within Schedule 2 of the Privacy Act', commenced on 10 June 2025. An individual may sue where the defendant invaded their privacy by 'intruding upon the individual's seclusion' or by misusing information relating to them, they 'would have had a reasonable expectation of privacy in all the circumstances', and 'the public interest in protecting their privacy outweighs any countervailing public interest'. Unlike the APPs, it is not limited by the small business exemption. AI uses that surveil individuals or generate or expose information about them (for example deepfakes) can engage it.
obligations.confidenceNote: Elements from the OAIC page (rank 2); the Schedule 2 text itself was not fetched, and the page does not state the intent/recklessness or seriousness elements that commentary describes. Treat as a lead until checked against Schedule 2. The statement that the small business exemption does not apply is from commentary and the structure of Schedule 2, to confirm. AI mapping is analytical.

obligations.instrument: OAIC Guidance on privacy and the use of commercially available AI products
obligations.citation: Guidance (whole), incl. 'Top five takeaways'; APPs 1, 3, 5, 6, 8, 10, 11
obligations.title: Privacy when deploying commercially available AI products (OAIC)
obligations.statement: Guidance for 'organisations that are deploying AI systems'. Its takeaways include that 'Privacy obligations will apply to any personal information input into an AI system', that organisations should 'update their privacy policies and notifications', that generating or inferring personal information with AI 'is a collection of personal information' under APP 3, that APP 6 limits use and disclosure to the primary purpose, and that as best practice organisations 'do not enter personal information, and particularly sensitive information, into publicly available generative AI tools'.
tierBasis: Privacy Act 1988 Sch 1 APPs 1, 3, 5, 6, 8, 10, 11 (binding on APP entities)
obligations.confidenceNote: The APPs bind APP entities; most businesses with annual turnover of $3 million or less are not APP entities (small business exemption), which counsel should check. Quoted fragments only; the guidance is longer.

obligations.instrument: OAIC Guidance on privacy and developing and training generative AI models
obligations.citation: Guidance (whole), incl. 'Top five takeaways'; APP 3.5 (fair means), APP 6, APP 10
obligations.title: Privacy when developing and training generative AI models (OAIC)
obligations.statement: Guidance 'intended for developers of generative artificial intelligence (AI) models or systems' subject to the Privacy Act. It states that 'Just because data is publicly available or otherwise accessible does not mean it can legally be used' to train models, that sensitive information generally needs consent, that developers 'must take reasonable steps to ensure accuracy' (APP 10), and that 'the creation of a dataset through web scraping may constitute a covert and therefore unfair means of collection' under APP 3.5.
tierBasis: Privacy Act 1988 Sch 1 APPs 3, 6, 10 (binding on APP entities)
obligations.confidenceNote: Addressed to developers, including organisations that fine-tune or train models on data they hold. Small business exemption as above.

obligations.instrument: Workplace Surveillance Act 2005 (NSW)
obligations.citation: s 3 ('computer surveillance'); s 10(1), (2) (14 days' written notice); s 12(a) (in accordance with a computer surveillance policy)
obligations.title: Notice and policy for computer surveillance of employees (NSW)
obligations.statement: 'Computer surveillance' is surveillance 'by means of software or other equipment that monitors or records the information input or output, or other use, of a computer' (s 3). 'Surveillance of an employee must not commence without prior notice in writing to the employee', given 'at least 14 days before the surveillance commences' unless the employee agrees to less (s 10(1), (2)). Computer surveillance is not to be carried out unless it 'is carried out in accordance with a policy of the employer on computer surveillance of employees at work' (s 12(a)). AI tools that monitor or record staff use of computers, such as productivity analytics or copilot telemetry, can fall within these provisions.
obligations.confidenceNote: Quoted from the Act as made; the in-force consolidation could not be fetched. Check ss 3, 10 and 12 against the current version. Applies to employees at work in NSW. The AI mapping is analytical. Other states' surveillance laws not researched.

obligations.instrument: Defence Trade Controls Act 2012 (Cth), as amended by the Defence Trade Controls Amendment Act 2024
obligations.citation: s 10A(1) (supply of DSGL technology to a foreign person in Australia); see also ss 10B, 10C
obligations.title: Supplying controlled technology to foreign persons, including through AI tools
obligations.statement: Section 10A(1) makes it an offence for a person to supply 'DSGL technology to another person' who 'is a foreign person' where the supply occurs in Australia, without a permit under s 11 or an exemption ('Penalty: Imprisonment for 10 years or 2,500 penalty units, or both'). Supply includes 'the provision of access to DSGL technology'. Defence states the amendments took effect on 1 September 2024, alongside ss 10B (re-supply) and 10C (DSGL services). Placing controlled technical data into AI tools or models that foreign persons, or offshore providers, can reach may amount to supply.

keyDates.note: Per Defence; Schedule 1 commenced by Proclamation (F2024N00654)

obligations.confidenceNote: s 10A quoted from the amending Act as made (Sch 1 item 15); the current compilation of the principal Act was not fetched. Whether AI input is a 'supply' is for counsel; the mapping is analytical. Applies to anyone holding DSGL technology, not only defence suppliers.

obligations.instrument: Ahpra and National Boards: Meeting your professional obligations when using Artificial Intelligence in healthcare
obligations.citation: Guidance (whole): Accountability; Understanding; Transparency; Informed consent; Ethical and legal issues
obligations.title: Health practitioners' professional obligations when using AI (Ahpra)
obligations.statement: Ahpra and the National Boards explain how existing obligations in the Boards' codes of conduct apply when practitioners use AI, under the headings Accountability, Understanding, Transparency, Informed consent, and Ethical and legal issues. It states: 'Regardless of what technology is used in providing healthcare the practitioner remains responsible'.

keyDates.note: Page reviewed date; publication date not stated on the page

obligations.confidenceNote: Addressed to registered health practitioners, not organisations as such; mapped to healthServiceProvider so a health organisation's brief includes it. The codes of conduct are binding professional standards for practitioners; this guidance explains them.

obligations.instrument: Personal Data Protection Act 2012
obligations.citation: s 24 (Protection Obligation), as stated in PDPC Advisory Guidelines on Key Concepts, ch 17, paras 17.1-17.4
obligations.title: Protection of personal data, including data placed in AI systems (Singapore)
obligations.statement: The PDPC states that 'Section 24 of the PDPA requires an organisation to make reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data in its possession or under its control in order to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks' (para 17.1). What is reasonable depends on factors including 'the nature of the personal data', the form in which it is held and 'the possible impact to the individual concerned' (para 17.2), and on the organisation's size and whether a third party holds the data for it (para 17.4). Personal data placed in AI tools or held by AI providers falls within it.
obligations.confidenceNote: The Act's text on Singapore Statutes Online could not be fetched; s 24 is quoted as the PDPC states it in its advisory guidelines (2019 revision; a later consolidated edition of the guidelines exists). Check against the Act. AI mapping is analytical.

obligations.instrument: Personal Data Protection Act 2012, Part 6A, and Personal Data Protection (Notification of Data Breaches) Regulations 2021
obligations.citation: ss 26B, 26C, 26D(1)-(2); Regulations reg 4 (500 individuals)
obligations.title: Assessing and notifying data breaches within 3 calendar days (Singapore)
obligations.statement: Where an organisation assesses that a data breach is notifiable, it 'must notify the Commission as soon as is practicable, but in any case no later than 3 calendar days after the day the organisation makes that assessment' (s 26D(1)), and then notify affected individuals where the breach is likely to result in significant harm to them (s 26D(2)). A breach is notifiable if it is likely to result in significant harm, or is of significant scale: 'the prescribed number of affected individuals is 500' (reg 4). The PDPC guide states the assessment is to be made 'within 30 calendar days'. Breaches through AI tools or AI providers are assessed and notified on the same terms.
obligations.confidenceNote: Regulation 4 quoted from SSO. s 26D quoted from a LawPlayer mirror of the Act (rank 5) and consistent with the PDPC guide; check against SSO. The 30-day assessment period is from the PDPC guide (s 26C(3)).

obligations.instrument: Companies Act 1967
obligations.citation: s 157(1) (act honestly and use reasonable diligence)
obligations.title: Directors' duty of honesty and reasonable diligence (Singapore)
obligations.statement: Section 157(1) provides that 'A director must at all times act honestly and use reasonable diligence in the discharge of the duties of his or her office.' It does not mention AI; it addresses how directors oversee the company's affairs, including the adoption and control of AI.
obligations.confidenceNote: Quoted from a LawPlayer mirror (rank 5) that links to SSO; the SSO text could not be fetched. Expect the Fabric to hold this as a lead until checked against SSO.

obligations.instrument: Cybersecurity Act 2018, as amended by the Cybersecurity (Amendment) Act 2024
obligations.citation: s 14 (CII owner's duty to report cybersecurity incidents), as extended from 31 October 2025
obligations.title: CII owners report cybersecurity incidents within 2 hours (Singapore)
obligations.statement: The Cyber Security Agency states that from 31 October 2025 reporting by owners of critical information infrastructure covers 'incidents suspected of being caused by Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs)' and incidents 'that result in a disruption of essential services for non-interconnected systems under the CII owner's control', and that CII owners are to 'report such incidents to CSA within 2 hours of becoming aware of such an occurrence'. AI systems interconnected with CII, or relied on to deliver the essential service, are within this reporting.

keyDates.note: Key provisions of the Amendment Act (passed 7 May 2024) commenced

obligations.confidenceNote: From the regulator's release (rank 2); the Act's section text and the 2025 Regulations were not fetched, so the s 14 pinpoint is from commentary. AI mapping is analytical.

obligations.instrument: Strategic Goods (Control) Act 2002
obligations.citation: Intangible transfer of technology (ITT) permits, as administered by Singapore Customs
obligations.title: Permits for intangible transfer of controlled technology (Singapore)
obligations.statement: Singapore Customs describes intangible transfer of technology as 'the electronic transmission of controlled strategic goods technology from Singapore, such as through email or fax', including making controlled technology 'available on a computer or server in Singapore so that someone outside Singapore can access it'. A permit is needed to transmit strategic goods software or technology, or any software or technology under the catch-all provision. Placing controlled technology into AI tools hosted or reachable outside Singapore may be such a transfer.
obligations.confidenceNote: From the regulator's page (rank 2), which does not cite sections of the Act; the Act on SSO was not fetched. Applies to anyone transmitting controlled technology, not only defence suppliers. Whether AI input is a transfer is for counsel.

obligations.instrument: Workplace Fairness Act 2025 (with the Workplace Fairness (Dispute Resolution) Act)
obligations.citation: Act (whole): prohibition of discriminatory employment decisions; grievance handling processes
obligations.title: Fair employment decisions, including those made with AI tools (Singapore)
obligations.statement: The Ministry of Manpower states that the first Bill, covering the scope of protections and employers' obligations, was passed on 8 January 2025 and the Dispute Resolution Bill on 4 November 2025, and that 'We aim for the Act to take effect in end-2027'. The Act bars employers from making unfavourable employment decisions because of protected characteristics, and MOM states that employers are to put in place grievance handling processes. Employment decisions made or informed by AI hiring and assessment tools remain the employer's decisions.
obligations.confidenceNote: Commencement is a stated aim ('end-2027'), not a fixed date, so no commences date is recorded. Small-firm thresholds and the list of protected characteristics are from commentary, not verified. The AI link is analytical; the MOM pages do not mention AI.

obligations.instrument: Consumer Protection (Fair Trading) Act 2003
obligations.citation: Unfair practices (Part 2), as applied by CCCS to AI-generated fake reviews (Lambency Detailing, 3 July 2025)
obligations.title: Unfair practices, including AI-generated fake reviews (Singapore)
obligations.statement: The Competition and Consumer Commission of Singapore treated a business's posting of fake reviews, written with ChatGPT and attributed to customers without consent, as an 'unfair trade practice' under the Consumer Protection (Fair Trading) Act, and accepted undertakings to stop and remedy it. CCCS described it as 'the first case involving both a third-party platform and the use of AI to create these fake reviews'.
obligations.confidenceNote: The release does not cite section numbers; the CPFTA text (s 4 and the Second Schedule) was not fetched. Applies to suppliers dealing with consumers. Expect the Fabric to hold this as a lead until the Act's provisions are cited.

obligations.instrument: MOH and HSA Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare Guidelines (AIHGle 2.0), MOH circular MH 70:47/1 MOH-MHC-0024-2026
obligations.citation: Circular paras 1-5 and the Guidelines (whole)
obligations.title: AI in healthcare guidelines for licensees and professionals (Singapore)
obligations.statement: MOH circular dated 13 March 2026, addressed to 'All HCSA Licensees' and 'All Healthcare Professionals', announces AIHGle 2.0, co-developed with HSA and launched on 10 March 2026, building on the 2021 guidelines and covering generative AI. Its focus areas are 'Strengthening accountability through clarity of responsibilities for key stakeholders', 'Improving trust via guidance on transparency to facilitate informed decision-making', and updated guidance on assessing and mitigating deployment risks, with a deployers' toolkit.
obligations.confidenceNote: Quoted from the MOH circular (rank 2); the Guidelines document itself was not fetched. 'HCSA' is taken to be the Healthcare Services Act. The circular does not say whether the guidelines are mandatory; filed as Expected.

obligations.instrument: FSB Sound Practices for Responsible Adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI): Final report
obligations.citation: Sound Practices 1-12, esp. 1 (strategic direction and oversight), 10 (human oversight), 12 (third-party AI risk management)
obligations.title: FSB sound practices for responsible AI adoption by financial institutions
obligations.statement: Published 15 October 2026, the report 'sets out 12 sound practices financial institutions are encouraged to consider', and states that 'The board and senior management of financial institutions are strongly encouraged to reference the sound practices'. Sound Practice 1 is for the board and senior management to 'align AI adoption and governance with the financial institution's business model, risk appetite, and strategy'; Sound Practice 10 calls on institutions to 'implement appropriate and effective human oversight relevant to the materiality, risk' of each use; Sound Practice 12 to 'manage risks from third-party AI dependencies with a focus on performance, transparency, data quality'.
obligations.confidenceNote: From the FSB web page (rank 2); the PDF (https://www.fsb.org/uploads/P151026-1.pdf) could not be fetched. FSB practices bind no one directly; filed as Expected because they set out practices member authorities, including APRA and MAS, may draw on. The FSB is an international body, so jurisdiction INT.

MAS clarified in the final Guidelines that existing governance structures can be used and 'a dedicated AI committee is not required', and that basic AI policies may suffice where poor performance or unavailability is unlikely to have a material impact. Reviewer to consider adding that clarification to the statement; paragraph-level text of the final Guidelines not re-fetched.

CPG 230 and the Material Service Provider Register template were also amended. The page does not name the paragraphs; the record's statement is unchanged unless the cited contractual paragraphs are among those exempted.

The OAIC resources of 30 September 2026 (APP 1.7-1.9 Transparency Obligation Fact Sheet, Flowchart, and a Supplementary fact sheet for government agencies) are the guidance this record already holds; the obligation applies from 10 December 2026. No new record.
